newsitem.title: UK: UK inward investment mostly acquisitions -- Labour.
newsitem.headline: UK inward investment mostly acquisitions -- Labour.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party released figures on Monday, which it said exploded government claims about foreign investment in Britain.

Labour's employment spokesman Stephen Byers said the data countered ministers' claims that inward investment created new jobs and was attracted because the UK did not have a minimum wage and had opted out of the European Union Social Chapter which guarantees minimum employment rights.
In 1995, about 60 percent of all inward investment was due to British companies being acquired by foreign investors, not to investment in new factories creating new jobs, Byers said.

He said nearly one fifth of all inward investment was accounted for by just two acquisitions -- the 1.6 billion stg sale of Seeboard to Central and South West Corp and the 1.1 billion sale of South Western Electricity to another U.S. buyer, the Southern Company.

"The Tories constantly claim that the UK attracts inward investment because we have no minimum wage and have opted out of the Social Chapter," Byers said. "The reality is that the majority of inward investment comes from foreign investors making rich pickings from what's left of British industry.
"The government seeks to portray inward investment as being financial support for new businesses and extra jobs. In fact it is mainly the buying of shares and taking control of British companies."
